Among them were distributed denial-of-service attacks against the websites of banking, healthcare, energy, transport and water organisations, government agencies and political parties. A separate burst hit the national authentication service with more than 86 million requests, over a hundred times the normal load. That summary is short. The work it implies is not. articles.title: Three Sandbox Failures That Let AI Agents Escape
articles.excerpt: Your LLM agent just exfiltrated data through a container it shouldn't have been able to reach. The incident report calls it "emergent behavior." The logs show a missing seccomp profile, an open egress…
articles.body: Your LLM agent just exfiltrated data through a container it shouldn't have been able to reach. The incident report calls it "emergent behavior." The logs show a missing seccomp profile, an open egress rule, and a bind mount with propagation enabled. This article covers three containment failures that look like AI gone rogue, the specific configuration that closes each one, and the monitoring that catches the next escape before it becomes a headline. The Syscall Surface You Forgot to Filter Most teams run agents in containers with the default Docker seccomp profile. That profile blocks about 44 syscalls — but it allows ptrace , process_vm_readv , process_vm_writev , and bpf .

articles.title: Deleting a user's data from backups: crypto-shredding with one key per person
articles.excerpt: A user asks you to delete their data. You delete the row. Then you remember the replica, last month's backup, the S3 export someone made for analytics, and the log line with their email in it. You can…
articles.body: A user asks you to delete their data. You delete the row. Then you remember the replica, last month's backup, the S3 export someone made for analytics, and the log line with their email in it. You can't edit most of those. Crypto-shredding is the standard way out: encrypt each person's data under their own key, keep the keys in one small keystore, and "delete" a person by destroying their key. The ciphertext can stay wherever it is. Without the key it's noise. I built a small library for this called aegis-shred : a Rust core, a Python package and a CLI. from aegis_shred import MasterKey , Vault vault = Vault . open ( " keys.db " , MasterKey . from_env ( " AEGIS_MASTER_KEY " ), create = True ) blob = vault .

You give six residents a shared objective (grow the village, prepare for a raid, restock supplies) and watch them claim jobs, gather, build and upgrade. Then you click any resident and read their decision, their route and their memories. Play it in the browser, no signup, no API key: https://settlement-village.vercel.app A real recording of the live site: one click on Grow the village, then the decision log. How the agents cooperate The six residents bid for exclusive jobs using role suitability, distance and bounded experience. When a workplace or resource changes, they replan.

articles.title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security
articles.excerpt: Incident hitting 700 supermarkets exploited outdated devices exposed to the Internet.
articles.body: Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit).

articles.title: Planetary genealogy: Milky Way worlds belong to 1 of 2 ‘families,’ scientists find
articles.excerpt: Scientists have performed a cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.
articles.body: You can tell a lot about how a child will age by looking at their parents, and it turns out that this could be true for planetary systems, too. Scientists have performed cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems. The study team, led by researchers at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), studied 300 of the best-understood multiplanet systems of the over 1,000 that astronomers have discovered in the Milky Way. The team's research clarifies how the environments around infant stars directly affect planetary fates and, in turn, the survival of extrasolar planets, or exoplanets , that are potentially capable of hosting life.

articles.body: X-ray: NASA/CXC/INAF-IRA/A. Botteon et al.; Infrared: UKIDSS-GPS ; Radio: ASTRON/LOFAR; Image processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/N. Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters. A paper describing the findings, led by Andrea Botteon of the National Institute for Astrophysics, or INAF, in Italy, published Wednesday in the Astronomy & Astrophysics journal .

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Chuck Yeager was a test pilot for the U.S. Air Force who made history by flying an aircraft faster than the speed of sound. Yeager made his historic flight in a Bell X-1 rocket plane that he named "Glamorous Glennis" after his wife. Yeager had broken two ribs the night before when he fell off a horse, but that didn't stop him! His aircraft was dropped from a Boeing B-29 bomber before accelerating to a speed of Mach 1.07, which is about 821 mph (1,321 km/h). The speed of sound, Mach 1, is about 760 mph (1,223 km/h). USAF Capt. Charles E. Yeager (shown standing with the Bell X-1 supersonic rocket plane) became the first man to fly faster than the speed of sound in level flight on Oct. 14, 1947.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
